items.text: This teaching model uses a simulated hand to show how MRI turns magnetic resonance into an image.
These silver windings represent the main magnet. This model uses a steady current of 133 amperes.
This example receiver digitizes the radio-frequency voltage at 122.88 million samples per second.
A digital oscillator supplies sine and cosine references. Mixing shifts the signal toward baseband.
Filtering and decimation leave 32 thousand I and Q pairs per second in this example.
I and Q together describe the received signal, weighted by the coil sensitivity across the sample.
Within each tissue sample, transverse coherence decays while longitudinal magnetization recovers.
When the gradient stops, its frequency shift ends. The accumulated phase differences remain.
This pulse chiefly excites a 1500-hertz band, with a finite transition at the slice edges.
Farther off resonance, the pulse produces much less net tipping across the tissue.
A reversed z-gradient lobe supplies the rephasing area needed after this slice-selective pulse.
At the echo, the readout gradient refocuses its accumulated x phase, and the combined signal peaks.
The gradient pulse area sets ky, a spatial frequency measured in cycles per metre.
Combining the encodings estimates each voxel. Finite sampling sets the resolution and point-spread function.
Cortical bone has very short-lived signal. Tendons also appear dark with the timing used here.
These measurements and images were calculated from the simulated anatomy and acquisition.
